battle.title: Scheduler Showdown: Who Gets the CPU?
battle.description: FCFS, SJF and Round Robin face off in a fight for CPU time.

questions.text: Which scheduling policy can starve long jobs if short jobs keep arriving?
questions.explanation: SJF always prefers the job with the shortest burst, so a long job can wait forever behind a stream of short ones. Round Robin gives every process a turn, so it cannot starve anyone.

questions.text: One CPU-bound process with a huge burst arrives first, followed by many short I/O-bound processes, under FCFS. What is this problem called?
questions.explanation: Short processes pile up behind the long one and wait a long time, lowering utilization and raising average waiting time. Belady's anomaly and thrashing are memory-management issues, and priority inversion involves locks.

questions.text: Three processes arrive at time 0 with bursts 5, 3 and 2, served FCFS in that order. What does this program print?
questions.explanation: Waiting times are 0, 5 and 8, which sum to 13, and 13 / 3 = 4.33. Turnaround times (5, 8, 10) average 7.67, which is a different metric.

questions.text: An interactive time-sharing system must give every user a quick first response, even when many jobs are running. Which policy fits best?
options: Round Robin with a reasonably small time quantum
questions.answer: Round Robin with a reasonably small time quantum
questions.explanation: Round Robin cycles through all ready processes so each gets the CPU quickly, giving good response time. FCFS and non-preemptive SJF let one running job block everyone else until it finishes.

questions.text: In Round Robin, the time quantum is set larger than every process's burst time. How does the scheduler behave?
options: It never preempts and never finishes
It context switches more often than before
questions.explanation: No process ever uses up its quantum, so none is preempted and each runs to completion in arrival order, which is FCFS. A very small quantum causes the extra context switches, not a large one.

coding.title: Round Robin Average Waiting Time
coding.description: n processes all arrive at time 0 and sit in a ready queue in input order. The CPU runs the process at the front for min(q, remaining burst) time units; if it still has work left it goes to the back of the queue, otherwise it finishes. Waiting time of a process = completion time - burst time. Print the average waiting time over all processes, using String.format("%.2f", x).
coding.inputDescription: Line 1: n and the time quantum q. Line 2: n burst times.
coding.outputDescription: The average waiting time with exactly 2 decimal places.
